issues.legal_issue: A timely acquisition application made after confirmation of a purchase notice does not end the acquisition process, which remains subject to further acquisition timelines and the reservation-lapse mechanism.
material_facts: The landowner served a purchase notice because the land’s designation made it difficult to sell at its expected price, and the notice was confirmed.
The appropriate authority submitted an acquisition proposal within one year of confirmation, but no further action to acquire the land followed.
issues.conclusion: A timely application to acquire the land must be followed by acquisition under the applicable statutory scheme. Ordinarily, the State Government should make the acquisition declaration within one year of receiving the application; if it does not, an aggrieved person may ask a court to direct it to do so. If the plan has been in force for ten years, the further purchase-notice and lapse process must also be followed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 49(1) and 49(7) require a timely acquisition application after confirmation of a purchase notice, while Section 49(1) requires purchase in accordance with the Act. Sections 126(4) and 127 then govern further acquisition and lapse. The Court relied on Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra, (2007) 7 SCC 555, and Shrirampur Municipal Council v. Satyabhamabai Bhimaji Dawkher, (2013) 5 SCC 627, on the acquisition scheme and the meaning of steps towards acquisition; it distinguished Prakash R. Gupta v. Lonavala Municipal Council, (2009) 1 SCC 514.

predicates.confirmed_purchase_notice: The government confirmed a notice requiring the authority to purchase the affected land.
predicates.timely_acquisition_application: The appropriate authority applied to acquire the land within the time allowed after confirmation of the notice.
predicates.government_declaration_not_made_within_o: The government did not make the acquisition declaration within the ordinary period after receiving the application.

issues.definition: When a confirmed purchase notice is followed by a timely acquisition application but the government does not make its declaration within the ordinary time, the affected person may seek an immediate declaration.

issues.legal_issue: After a planning reservation has remained in force for the prescribed long period, a landowner must serve a further purchase notice before relying on the statutory process for lapse of the reservation.
material_facts: The development plan had been in force for more than ten years.
The landowner had served a purchase notice under the process applicable to a confirmed purchase notice, but had not served a further purchase notice after the plan had been in force for ten years.
The acquisition proposal was not followed by effective further steps to acquire the land.
issues.conclusion: In future cases, after ten years have elapsed from publication of the relevant plan, a second purchase notice must be served under Section 127. If the land is not acquired and effective acquisition steps are not commenced within one year after that notice, the reservation lapses. An application or other preliminary step that may not lead to acquisition is not, by itself, an effective step towards acquisition.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 126 and 127 require acquisition steps to be steps that can lead to acquisition; the mere making of an application or sending of a letter is insufficient. Under Section 127, after the prescribed period has elapsed, the owner must give notice and the authority must acquire the land or commence effective acquisition steps within the applicable period. The Court relied on the majority in Girnar Traders v. State of Maharashtra, (2007) 7 SCC 555, and Shrirampur Municipal Council v. Satyabhamabai Bhimaji Dawkher, (2013) 5 SCC 627. It read Hasmukhrai V. Mehta v. State of Maharashtra, (2015) 3 SCC 154, as having granted relief on its exceptional facts under Article 142, where no further notice had been served.

rule.if: planning_reservation_lapse_dispute and plan_in_force_for_prescribed_long_period and second_purchase_notice_served and (land_not_acquired or no_effective_acquisition_steps)

predicates.planning_reservation_lapse_dispute: The case concerns whether a planning reservation over land has lapsed.
predicates.plan_in_force_for_prescribed_long_period: The plan containing the reservation has remained in force for the period after which the owner may invoke the statutory lapse process.
predicates.second_purchase_notice_served: The owner served a further notice seeking acquisition or release of the land after that period elapsed.
predicates.land_not_acquired: The authority did not acquire the land within the period following the further notice.
predicates.no_effective_acquisition_steps: The authority did not commence steps that could lead to acquisition within the period following the further notice.

issues.definition: When a planning-reservation dispute concerns a plan that has remained in force for the prescribed long period, a further notice is served, and the land is neither acquired nor subject to effective acquisition steps, the reservation lapses.

issues.legal_issue: An exceptionally prolonged failure to acquire land after a confirmed purchase notice may justify release of the land as complete justice, even though the landowner did not serve the further notice ordinarily required for statutory lapse.
material_facts: The plan had been in force for fifteen years, and more than ten years had passed since the purchase notice was served and confirmed.
The appropriate authority made an acquisition proposal within the required time, but nothing further was done to acquire the land.
No court had stayed the acquisition process.
The landowner had not served a further purchase notice under the ordinary lapse process.
issues.conclusion: In order to do complete justice under Article 142, the Court held that the reservation and acquisition proposal had lapsed on these exceptional facts, despite the absence of a further purchase notice. The Court clarified that future cases must follow the further-notice process.
issues.legal_principle: Article 142 permitted the Court to do complete justice in this case in light of the inordinately long delay and the absence of any stay or meaningful progress after the acquisition proposal. The Court referred to Hasmukhrai V. Mehta v. State of Maharashtra, (2015) 3 SCC 154, and read its exceptional result as relief under Article 142; it also stated that the ordinary scheme of Sections 49, 126 and 127 requires a further notice for lapse in future cases.

rule.if: planning_reservation_appeal and confirmed_purchase_notice and timely_acquisition_proposal and prolonged_inaction_after_proposal and no_court_stay

predicates.planning_reservation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning a planning reservation over land.
predicates.confirmed_purchase_notice: The government confirmed a notice requiring the authority to purchase the affected land.
predicates.timely_acquisition_proposal: The appropriate authority proposed acquisition within the time allowed after confirmation of the notice.
predicates.prolonged_inaction_after_proposal: After making the proposal, the authority took no further action to acquire the land for an exceptionally long period.
predicates.no_court_stay: No court order stayed the acquisition process during the period of inaction.

issues.definition: In a planning-reservation appeal, a timely acquisition proposal followed by exceptionally prolonged inaction and no court stay may result in the reservation and proposal lapsing as complete justice, even after a confirmed purchase notice.
